headline: Anak Krakatau Eruption Disrupts Hundreds of Flights at Jakarta’s Main Airport
seoTitle: Anak Krakatau Eruption Disrupts Jakarta Airport Flights | FMB News
seoDescription: Volcanic ash from Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau eruption disrupted hundreds of flights at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta airport on September 6, 2026. The situation remains developing.
deck: Volcanic ash from Anak Krakatau forced flight suspensions at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and other Indonesian airports, disrupting hundreds of services as authorities monitored a continuing eruption.
author: FMB News Desk

sections.heading: What happened
paragraphs: Indonesia’s Anak Krakatau volcano continued erupting on September 6, sending volcanic ash across parts of western Indonesia and forcing flight suspensions at Jakarta’s Soekarno-Hatta International Airport and several other airports.

Reuters reported that 301 flights at Soekarno-Hatta, including 58 international services, had been affected, citing airport operator Angkasa Pura. Associated Press separately reported widespread airport disruption as ash spread across the region.

Singapore Airlines and AirAsia issued their own advisories confirming cancellations or schedule changes involving Jakarta because of volcanic ash. The eruption and aviation disruption remain active and flight status can change quickly.
This is a developing story. FMB News will update this report as verified information becomes available.

sections.heading: Context
paragraphs: Anak Krakatau sits in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra and has been erupting since late September 4 into September 6. Indonesian authorities detected volcanic ash at Jakarta’s main airport early Sunday, prompting repeated extensions of flight restrictions as conditions evolved.

Volcanic ash poses a serious aviation hazard because fine particles can damage aircraft engines and other systems. Indonesian disaster and transport authorities have continued monitoring ash movement and airport conditions.

Authorities said there was no imminent tsunami threat from the current eruption in reporting reviewed by FMB News. That assessment should not be confused with the deadly 2018 Anak Krakatau event, when a flank collapse generated a tsunami along nearby coasts.

sections.heading: Why this matters to Filipinos
paragraphs: Jakarta is a major Southeast Asian business and travel hub. Filipinos flying to Indonesia, connecting through Jakarta, or traveling on regional itineraries that depend on Jakarta aircraft rotations may face delays, cancellations or rebooking even when their own route is not directly named in an initial advisory.

The disruption also matters to Philippine travelers using Singapore, Kuala Lumpur and other regional hubs because airlines may reposition aircraft and crews as schedules recover. Passengers should rely on their operating airline and airport status notices rather than assume previously issued departure times remain valid.

sections.heading: What remains unclear
paragraphs: The exact time normal operations will fully resume at Soekarno-Hatta and the other affected airports remains subject to ash conditions and aviation safety assessments.

The final number of cancelled, delayed or diverted flights may rise as airlines update schedules. FMB News has not verified a specific Philippine carrier cancellation attributable to Anak Krakatau in this reporting pass and is not claiming one.

sections.heading: What to watch next
paragraphs: Watch for updated Indonesian aviation notices on airport reopening, further eruptions or changes in ash-plume direction, and airline-specific advisories for flights to, from or through Jakarta.
Philippine passengers with Indonesia travel should check their airline’s official flight-status channel before leaving for the airport and confirm any connection affected by Jakarta operations.

verificationNotes: Reuters reported 301 affected flights at Soekarno-Hatta, including 58 international services, citing airport operator Angkasa Pura; Associated Press independently confirmed broad airport disruption from the eruption.
Singapore Airlines and AirAsia published their own operational advisories confirming Jakarta cancellations or schedule changes caused by volcanic ash.
FMB News did not find an earlier matching Anak Krakatau article in the repository before publication, so this is not being treated as a continuation.
The article does not claim that a Philippine carrier has cancelled a flight because no such carrier-specific cancellation was independently verified in this pass.
The situation is labeled DEVELOPING because airport reopening times, ash movement and final disruption totals can change.
